source: Cloudflare WAF attack-pattern taxonomy, curated in-house. Category names confirmed 2026-08-24 against the team's own behaviour-pattern export: PathTraversal, KnownCVE_Signature, SSRF, NoSQLi, OpenRedirect, SensitivePathAccess, XSS, SQLi, RCE_CommandInjection. Those nine are the ones that fired for the one client dataset available; docs/BLUEPRINT.md refers to fifteen, so six are not represented there yet. Add categories as entries in this file; scripts/seed_taxonomy.py upserts by slug, so re-running never duplicates.

schema_notes.detection_logic: Sigma-flavoured selection blocks, kept as data rather than a query string so the Phase 3 taxonomy matcher and the Phase 4 backtest can both read it. Modifiers follow Sigma syntax: field|contains, field|re, field|startswith.
schema_notes.required_fields: Fields that must exist in the sample for this entry to be feasible at all. Drives the Phase 2 'reassess data & patterns' check.
schema_notes.suggested_rule_type: Hint for the Phase 3 classifier, not a substitute for it.

entries.name: Cloudflare WAF - SQL injection attempt against public web application
entries.description: SQL injection payloads in the request path, query string, or body, seen either as a WAF managed-rule block or as raw SQL syntax in the query string when the WAF is in log-only mode. Maps to the in-house category 'SQLi'. NoSQL injection is a separate category ('NoSQLi') in that taxonomy and is deliberately not covered here: its payloads are operator syntax inside JSON, not SQL keywords, and folding them together would make both harder to tune.
assumptions: ClientRequestQuery is URL-decoded during ingestion. Undecoded, '+' stands in for a space and the \s in this regex stops matching: on the shipped fixture that costs 1 of 5 SQLi events.

RuleID scopes the waf_managed_block branch to the SQLi managed rules. Without it the branch fires on every WAF block, SQLi or not. The value here, 100015, is a placeholder from the shipped fixture and has NOT been confirmed against a real ruleset. Checked 2026-08-24: the team's production Cloudflare data reaches Sentinel as the HTTP-requests dataset, which carries no RuleID field at all, so there was nothing to confirm it against. This branch therefore only applies to a firewall_events-shaped log; for the HTTP-requests shape the equivalent discriminator is WAFSQLiAttackScore, and 'cloudflare-waf-low-attack-score-not-blocked' covers that path.

The pattern is written for Lucene's regex engine, which is what Elastic uses and which is not PCRE. Three things follow. It is wrapped in .* because Lucene anchors a pattern to the whole field value. \s is spelled [ \t] because a backslash escape in Lucene is a literal character, not a class - the field arrives URL-decoded, so a real space or tab is what appears. And case-insensitivity is spelled as [uU][nN]... rather than (?i), which Lucene rejects as a parse error. A lowercase ingest processor on the field would let all of that collapse back to plain lowercase literals.

One narrowing, deliberate: \bor\b became [^a-zA-Z]or, because Lucene has no word boundary. A query string whose value *begins* with 'or 1=1' and has nothing in front of it is therefore missed. In a real query string the value is always preceded by '=' or '&', so this costs the case where the whole field is the payload and nothing else.

This logic is written for log analysis, keying on ClientRequestPath and ClientRequestQuery separately as Logpush firewall_event delivers them. The team's own Cloudflare custom rules match http.request.uri, path and query combined; if this entry is ever turned into a custom rule, the fields have to be joined.

If deployed as a Cloudflare custom rule rather than an Elastic one: the regex operator 'matches' is Enterprise-plan only, and Cloudflare's engine is RE2, which has no backreferences and no lookaround. This pattern uses neither, so it ports as written.
false_positives: Scheduled DAST/pentest windows against the same hostname
Search boxes and CMS admin tooling that legitimately pass SQL-like strings in the query
Security researchers on a bug bounty scope
entries.author: IMS team
entries.notes: Single-event field match, so custom query is enough; escalate to threshold only if the client wants volume-based alerting instead of per-request. Action 'log' is deliberately in scope: a WAF in log-only mode still evidences the attempt, and arguably matters more because nothing stopped it. That also matches the team's documented rollout practice, which runs a new custom rule in Log for several days before switching it to Block.

entries.name: Cloudflare WAF - credential stuffing / password spraying against login endpoint
entries.description: Repeated failed POSTs to an authentication endpoint from a single client IP or ASN within a short window. Distinguished from a single brute force by breadth: many usernames, few attempts each. NOT confirmed against the in-house taxonomy: its nine observed categories are all payload-pattern web attacks, and none of them is credential stuffing or brute force. This entry was written as a second structural example, to exercise the threshold rule type alongside the single-event one. Treat its logic as a proposal, not as codified team knowledge.

detection_logic.condition: login_attempt and failed | count() by ClientIP >= 20 within 5m

false_positives: Mobile apps retrying with a stale token after a password change
Corporate NAT / proxy egress IPs where many real users share one ClientIP
Load tests and synthetic monitoring hitting the login endpoint
entries.source_project: proposed, not yet in the in-house taxonomy
entries.author: IMS team
entries.notes: Threshold needs a per-client baseline: check the sample's normal failed-login rate per IP before committing to count_gte=20. Behind heavy NAT, group by ClientIP + ClientRequestUserAgent instead.

entries.name: Cloudflare WAF - path traversal attempt
entries.description: Directory traversal in the request path or query string, across the encoding variants used to evade a single decoding layer: literal ../, single and double URL encoding, Windows backslash, and overlong UTF-8. CWE-22. Maps to the in-house category 'PathTraversal'. Ported from the team's own reviewed Cloudflare custom-rule pattern.
assumptions: The source rule matches http.request.uri, path and query together. Logpush delivers those as two fields, so the same list is applied to each and the results OR'd. Matching the path alone would miss payloads in the query string, which the source document calls mandatory to cover.

Written as a literal list rather than a regex, because every branch of the original was a literal. Elastic's regex engine is Lucene's, which is anchored to the whole field value and has no inline flags, so the regex form drafted a query that could not run; a contains list converts to wildcards, which Lucene does support. Nothing about what this matches changed.

Both cases of each percent-encoding are listed. Sigma matches values case-insensitively, so one form would be enough for the taxonomy matcher and the backtest, but the Lucene query those convert to is case-sensitive. Listing both is what makes the generated query agree with the entry.

If ported back to a Cloudflare custom rule: the 'matches' operator is Enterprise-plan only, and RE2 supports no backreferences or lookaround. This pattern used neither, and as a literal list the question no longer arises.
false_positives: Internal vulnerability scanners and scheduled DAST windows against the same hostname
Application endpoints that legitimately carry encoded path fragments in a parameter
entries.author: IMS team
entries.notes: Known gaps recorded by the pattern's author and deliberately not silently fixed here: URL-encoded backslash (%5c / %5C) is not covered, and only one overlong UTF-8 variant is, so %e0%80%ae and mixed forms like %c0%2e slip past. Overlong UTF-8 in a URL is close to a certain indicator on its own; a legitimate client never sends it.

entries.name: Cloudflare WAF - sensitive path and config file access
entries.description: Requests for configuration, VCS and credential artefacts that should never be reachable over HTTP: .env, .git/, .aws/credentials, id_rsa, web.config and similar. CWE-538 and CWE-548. Maps to the in-house category 'SensitivePathAccess'. Ported from the team's own reviewed Cloudflare custom-rule pattern.
assumptions: Path only, not the query string. That is what the source rule does, because these are filenames rather than payloads.

wp-admin and wp-login stay in scope even where the client runs no WordPress. That is the point: on a non-WordPress site such a request is a strong signal of a generic scanner, since mass scanning does not know the target's stack.

Written as a literal list rather than a regex, because every branch of the original was a literal. Elastic's regex engine is Lucene's, which is anchored to the whole field value and reads $ as a literal character, so the regex form drafted a query that could not run.

.env is matched with endswith rather than contains, which is what the original's '\.env$|\.env\?' was for: it keeps .env.example and .env.sample out. The '?' half of that alternation is dropped because it only mattered when path and query were one field; ClientRequestPath never contains a query string.

Sigma matches values case-insensitively but the Lucene query it converts to is case-sensitive, so a request for /.ENV would be caught by the taxonomy matcher and missed by the drafted rule. Unlike the percent-encodings in the path-traversal entry, filename case is not varied often enough to be worth doubling every literal; add the variant if a client's traffic shows it.
false_positives: Internal monitoring or deployment tooling that requests build artefacts by path
Developer tools pointed at a production host by mistake
entries.author: IMS team
entries.notes: Recorded by the pattern's author as worth adding but not yet added: .htaccess (only .htpasswd is covered), common backup artefacts (.bak, .old, .sql, backup.zip), and framework debug endpoints (/actuator, /telescope, /_profiler, /server-status, /phpinfo.php, /adminer.php). Also noted: .git/HEAD is more specific and lower false-positive than \.git/ on its own. Volume here is usually recon; pairing with a rate-limit rule catches the campaign better than the pattern alone.

entries.name: Cloudflare WAF - RCE and command injection attempt
entries.description: Command chaining, shell substitution, PHP execution sinks, expression injection including the Log4Shell shape, CRLF command injection and encoded PowerShell. CWE-78 and CWE-95. Maps to the in-house category 'RCE_CommandInjection'. Ported from the team's own reviewed Cloudflare custom-rule pattern, including the two corrections its author made before implementation.
assumptions: The source rule matches http.request.uri, path and query together; the same pattern is applied to each Logpush field and OR'd. The document calls covering the query string mandatory here, because that is where the payload usually sits.

Two corrections the pattern's author had already made are carried over: passwthru is spelled passthru, which is the real PHP function and without which that branch could never match anything; and the greedy ${.*} is bounded to ${[^}]{1,100}}, which stops it swallowing an unrelated span of a large JSON body.

The pattern is written for Lucene's regex engine, which is what Elastic uses and which is not PCRE. It is wrapped in .* because Lucene anchors to the whole field value; \s is spelled [ \t] because a backslash escape there is a literal character rather than a class; and case-insensitivity is spelled [sS][yY]... rather than (?i), which Lucene rejects as a parse error. The ${[^}]{1,100}} and `[^`]*` branches are unchanged - negated character classes and bounded repetition are both things Lucene has.

One narrowing, deliberate: \bsystem(, \bexec(, \bpassthru( and \bshell_exec( became [^a-zA-Z]system( and so on, because Lucene has no word boundary. A field whose value *begins* with one of those sinks and has nothing in front of it is missed. It also still refuses 'ecosystem(', which is what the boundary was there for.
%0a is spelled %0[aA] rather than relying on the old (?i) to cover %0A.
If ported back to a Cloudflare custom rule: 'matches' is Enterprise-plan only, and RE2 has no backreferences or lookaround. This pattern uses neither.
false_positives: API endpoints that legitimately accept ${...} template syntax or backticks in a parameter; whitelist those endpoints explicitly rather than weakening the pattern
Security testing windows and internal tooling that sends shell-like strings
entries.author: IMS team
entries.notes: Confidence is lower than the other two ported patterns because ${...} can still over-match on request bodies even when bounded. Sinks the author recorded as not yet covered: eval(, assert(, base64_decode( (common webshell obfuscation), proc_open(, popen(, Runtime.exec (Java), os.system and subprocess. (Python - the pattern detects the word python as a command but not Python code injection). No explicit reverse-shell indicators either (/bin/bash -i, nc -e, bash -c, 0<&196).

entries.name: Cloudflare WAF - low attack score request that reached the origin
entries.description: A request Cloudflare's ML scored as very likely malicious that was nonetheless not blocked or challenged, so the payload reached the origin server. Ported from the team's own two-tier attack-score runbook; this entry is its Tier 1, where a single event is enough to alert. Attack Score is the signal that catches payloads fuzzed just enough to miss a managed-rule signature, which is precisely what a signature-based entry cannot see.
assumptions: The score runs the counter-intuitive way: 1-99 where LOWER means more likely an attack. 20 is the team's threshold and also Cloudflare's own suggested starting point.

Numeric scores are Enterprise-plan only. On Business the only field is WAFAttackScoreClass, categorical: Clean / Likely clean / Likely attack / Attack. Substitute WAFAttackScoreClass == 'Attack' there. Cloudflare puts 'Likely attack' at 21-50 but does not publish exact class-to-score boundaries, so that substitution is close, not a 1:1 mapping.

Even on Enterprise the field only reaches Sentinel if it was selected when the Logpush job was set up. If the column is absent from the table entirely, a query referencing it errors rather than returning nothing, so check field existence before running anything against it.
A record with no WAFAction is treated here as not mitigated, which is the unsafe direction. Absent is not the same as allowed; if the export can omit the field, confirm before trusting the count.
false_positives: Internal scanners, partner testing, and scheduled pentest windows. The runbook keeps an explicit allowlist for these and ships it empty, so it has to be filled per client before go-live
entries.source_project: internal - Cloudflare WAF attack-score runbook, Tier 1
entries.author: IMS team
entries.notes: Severity per the source runbook: Critical when WAFRCEAttackScore is also <= 20, since that indicates RCE reaching the origin; High otherwise. Tier 2 of that runbook is deliberately NOT represented here: it needs at least 5 hits at score <= 20 spread across at least 3 distinct days in a rolling 14-day window, and this entry's aggregation format can express a count inside a window but not a count of distinct active days. Tier 2 stays a Sentinel analytic.
